notes: Environmental prosecution JR; magistrates' preliminary ruling jurisdiction quashed and ECJ reference ordered by consent.

enrichment.short_title: Thames Water v Bromley: magistrates' jurisdiction and sewage as directive waste
key_facts: Thames Water was prosecuted by the Environment Agency for 15 offences including 11 under section 33 EPA 1990 relating to sewage escaping from its network.
A preliminary issue arose whether sewage from a statutory sewerage undertaker's pipes is controlled waste for section 33 purposes even if the facts alleged were proved.
District Judge Carr at Havering held he had no jurisdiction to determine the preliminary point of law, limiting such rulings to abuse of process.
Both prosecution and defendant agreed he did have jurisdiction and invited the Divisional Court to decide the substantive waste question.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a magistrates' court refusal to determine a preliminary point of law in environmental prosecutions.
enrichment.outcome: The refusal to exercise jurisdiction was quashed; by consent the court referred two questions to the Court of Justice on whether escaped sewage amounts to directive waste under the Waste Framework Directive.
enrichment.ratio: A magistrates' court had jurisdiction to rule on a preliminary point of law not requiring findings of fact even before sections 8A and 8B Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 came into force; where remittal would serve no purpose CPR 54.19 permits the reviewing court to resolve the legal question or refer it to the ECJ.
legal_issues: Whether a district judge could determine a preliminary point of law in criminal proceedings
Whether sewage escaping from a statutory undertaker's network is directive waste under Directive 75/442/EEC
Whether article 2 exclusions under the Waste Framework Directive and Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive apply

confidence.notes: Jurisdictional ruling and ECJ reference are clearly recorded; substantive waste classification awaits CJEU determination.

notes: Income Support transitional housing costs; constructive abandonment after partner's child sex offences clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: SS v W: constructive abandonment for income support housing costs

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefit Act 1992

key_facts: Mrs W claimed income support in February 2002 while her husband faced charges for sexual offences against children including his nieces.
Bail conditions required him to live away from the matrimonial home; he was later imprisoned for five years.
The Secretary of State treated her mortgage housing costs as new housing costs because she had not been abandoned within Schedule 3 paragraph 8(3)(b).
Commissioner Rowland held constructive abandonment could be inferred from the nature of the offences and the impossibility of resumed cohabitation with young children.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Social Security Commissioner Rowland on the meaning of abandonment in income support transitional protection for housing costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the claimant was abandoned or constructively abandoned by the date of claim so existing-housing-costs treatment applied.
enrichment.ratio: Abandoned in Schedule 3 bears the same meaning as desertion in matrimonial law, including constructive abandonment where a partner's conduct would compel any reasonable spouse to end cohabitation; what matters is the abandoning party's intention, not the claimant's wish to treat the relationship as continuing.
legal_issues: Whether abandonment in paragraph 8(3)(b) includes constructive abandonment
Whether bail conditions or imprisonment can satisfy the physical separation element
Whether abandonment must be established at the date of the income support claim
Whether the claim must be solely because of abandonment
linked_authorities: Sickert v Sickert [1899] P 272
Ingram v Ingram [1956] P 390
Lang v Lang [1955] AC 402

notes: Cerebral palsy quantum trial; Sowden v Lodge burden of proof on local authority contribution applied.

enrichment.short_title: Walton v Calderdale: periodical payments and local authority care contribution
key_facts: Louis Walton, born July 1995, suffered dyskinetic cerebral palsy from perinatal asphyxia; liability was admitted and quantum alone remained.
The parties agreed a £2.65m package but disputed periodical payments for care after age 19, experts agreeing £50,548 per annum indexed.
The NHS trust argued local authority contribution should reduce payments to £44,000 but adduced no evidence and could not explain a Treasury publication relied on.
The litigation friend preferred periodical payments to protect lifelong care funding against inflation and capital depletion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on quantum of periodical payments for future care costs under the Damages Act 1996 after agreed settlement of other heads of damage.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant entitled to periodical payments at £50,548 per annum with RPI escalation from age 19; defendants failed to prove any local authority would meet care costs.
enrichment.ratio: The correct question is what is required to meet the claimant's reasonable care needs; a defendant asserting local authority provision must adduce cogent evidence and bears the burden of showing such provision, following Sowden v Lodge.
legal_issues: Whether periodical payments were appropriate for lifelong care after age 19
Whether local authority contribution should reduce the defendant's periodical payment liability
Which party bears the burden of proof on future public-sector care provision
Whether continuity of payment from a health service body satisfied section 2(3)
linked_authorities: Sowden v Lodge [2005] 1 All ER 583

confidence.notes: Single remaining issue, agreed expert figure and explicit burden-of-proof ruling are clearly recorded.

notes: Landmark Douglas/Hello privacy appeal; detailed analysis of confidence, commercial interest and economic torts.

enrichment.short_title: Douglas v Hello: wedding photographs, privacy and commercial confidence
key_facts: Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta-Jones sold OK! magazine exclusive rights to publish approved wedding photographs for £1m and imposed strict security at the Plaza Hotel reception.
A paparazzo infiltrated the event and Hello! published six unauthorised photographs before OK!'s authorised edition appeared.
Lindsay J awarded the Douglases £14,600 for privacy/confidence breach and OK! over £1m for commercial confidence and tortious interference.
Hello! appealed on liability and quantum; OK! and the Douglases cross-appealed on economic torts and a notional licence fee.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeals from liability and damages judgments after surreptitious publication of celebrity wedding photographs.
enrichment.outcome: Hello!'s appeal on the Douglases' privacy claim dismissed; appeal on OK!'s commercial confidence claim allowed; OK!'s economic tort cross-appeal and licence-fee cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Information about a wedding can be private and protected by confidence even where the claimants contracted to publish approved photographs; photographs are especially intrusive, but a commercial interest in wedding information akin to a trade secret does not extend OK!'s confidence rights against Hello! as the judge found.
legal_issues: Whether wedding information remained private despite the OK! exclusive publication contract
Whether the Douglases had a protectable commercial interest in wedding information
Whether the OK! contract extended confidence protection to OK! against Hello!
Whether Hello! committed unlawful interference with business by publishing the photographs
linked_authorities: Douglas v Hello! Ltd (No 3) [2003] 3 All ER 996
Campbell v MGN Ltd [2004] UKHL 22

notes: Neighbour right-of-way interlocutory appeal; Cobbold principle applied to late witness statement admission.

enrichment.short_title: Roberts v Williams: late witness statement in neighbour right-of-way dispute
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Roberts retained a right of way over Beechways after selling it to Mr and Mrs Williams, who built a wall and placed boulders allegedly encroaching on the route.
Mr Williams' exchanged statement referred to a May 2002 meeting with the claimants' solicitor; Mrs Williams later sought to add telephone conversations confirming permission to build.
District Judge Godwin refused admission six weeks before trial; HHJ Denyer dismissed the appeal though the trial had already been adjourned.
Brooke LJ granted second appeal on case management, medical confidentiality and whether evidence should be admitted with costs sanctions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second interlocutory appeal on permission to adduce a late witness statement and amend defences in a county court neighbour dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendants permitted to amend to plead estoppel/consent and to adduce Mrs Williams' evidence, with costs consequences for their procedural defaults.
enrichment.ratio: Under the CPR overriding objective amendments and late evidence should generally be allowed so the real dispute can be decided where prejudice can be cured by costs and the efficient administration of justice is not significantly harmed; excluding material evidence on permission issues that would in any event be explored at trial was wrong in principle.
legal_issues: Whether a district judge erred in refusing a late witness statement before trial
Whether medical confidentiality conditions prevented consideration of Mrs Williams' ill health
Whether defendants should have been permitted to amend to plead estoppel or consent
Appellate interference with case management discretion

key_facts: Claimants sued neighbours for interfering with a retained access drive at Beechways, Haverfordwest, after boulders and a wall were erected in 2002.

enrichment.ratio: Case management refusals of late evidence must balance Article 6 fairness with Cobbold principles favouring adjudication on the real issues where delay can be compensated in costs and trial length impact is modest.

notes: Important IAT jurisdiction judgment post-2002 Act; grounds must identify point of law and cannot be supplemented.

enrichment.short_title: Miftari v SSHD: IAT jurisdiction and Article 3 medical removal to Kosovo
key_facts: Mr Miftari, a 58-year-old Kosovan with PTSD, resisted removal on Article 3 and 8 grounds because of inadequate mental health services in Gjilan municipality.
The adjudicator found an exceptional case and allowed the appeal; the IAT reversed, holding he should have considered return to Kosovo generally.
The Secretary of State's grounds to the IAT challenged regional limitation of medical evidence but did not identify misunderstanding of Articles 3 and 8 jurisprudence.
The Court of Appeal held the IAT lacked jurisdiction because no error of law was properly formulated in the grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal on jurisdiction after post-2002 restriction to appeals on points of law only.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; IAT determination quashed for want of jurisdiction; adjudicator's allowance of the appeal remained in force.
enrichment.ratio: After the 2002 Act the IAT has jurisdiction only if the grounds of appeal identify a point of law; an objective error of law not pleaded in the grounds cannot confer jurisdiction, and the IAT cannot rehear facts unless the legal error disposes of the case on findings already made.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT had jurisdiction where grounds did not identify a point of law
Whether an adjudicator's misunderstanding of Article 3 and 8 jurisprudence was an error of law
Whether limiting medical analysis to Gjilan was an error of law or fact
Extent of IAT power to receive fresh evidence on a point of law appeal
linked_authorities: Mlauzi v Secretary of State [2005] EWCA Civ 128
N v Secretary of State [2004] 1 WLR 1182
R (Razgar) v Secretary of State [2004] 2 AC 368

notes: TCGA s253 qualifying loan appeal; refinancing purpose traced to original borrowing clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Robson v HMRC: qualifying loan and guarantee relief under section 253 TCGA
key_facts: Mr Robson guaranteed a Barclays loan refinancing his company's £251,000 overdraft and later paid £161,000 from farm sale proceeds to reduce the debt.
He sought allowable loss relief under section 253(4) for irrecoverable guaranteed amounts after the company failed.
General Commissioners found the loan was not used wholly for the company's trade because Queen Street works lacked contracts and appeared to benefit Mr Robson personally.
Patten J upheld the Commissioners' tracing of the rescheduled loan to the original overdraft purpose.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Patten J on whether a rescheduled company loan was a qualifying loan for capital gains tax guarantee relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Loan was not a qualifying loan because underlying overdraft funds were not shown to have been used wholly for the company's trade.
enrichment.ratio: Where borrowed money repays existing indebtedness, the new loan inherits the character of the original borrowing for section 253(1)(a); refinancing cannot convert a non-qualifying debt into a qualifying loan, and the guarantor bears the onus of proving trade purpose.
legal_issues: Whether section 253 looks at the purpose of the rescheduled loan or the original overdraft
Meaning of used wholly for the purposes of a trade in section 253(1)(a)
Whether wholly refers to quantum or exclusivity of purpose compared with wholly and exclusively
Standard of review of General Commissioners' findings of fact
linked_authorities: Strong & Co of Romsey Ltd v Woodifield [1906] AC 448
Edwards v Bairstow [1956] AC 14

notes: Renewed permission application on Somalia/Eyle clan asylum; Brooke LJ applies post-2002 IAT law-of-law threshold.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmed v SSHD: Somalia Eyle clan asylum and Article 3 permission
key_facts: The appellant, a Somali Eyle sub-clan member born 1985, fled to Ethiopia in 1991 and claimed asylum in October 2002 after militia attacks on his refugee camp.
The adjudicator distinguished unstarred IAT decisions in Abdi Ali and G and found no Convention refugee status or Article 3 breach on return to Somalia.
The IAT agreed Ethiopia camp violence was not necessarily indicative of treatment on return to Somalia and that G turned on risks to unaccompanied women.
On renewed application Brooke LJ refused permission, finding no real prospect of showing an IAT error of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from an IAT dismissal of an asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal dismissed; no real prospect of success on a point of law against the IAT determination.
enrichment.ratio: Where the IAT correctly reviewed points of law under its limited post-2002 jurisdiction and distinguished prior tribunal decisions on clan and gender risk, a further appeal requires identification of a legal error rather than fresh country evidence or merits reconsideration.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in treating Ethiopia camp attacks as irrelevant to Somalia return risk
Proper distinction of Abdi Ali and G on Eyle clan vulnerability
Article 3 threshold for internally displaced young men returning to Somalia
Whether fresh country information could succeed on a second appeal limited to law

notes: Financial Ombudsman causation challenge; ombudsman may depart from English law if fair and reasonable after taking law into account.

enrichment.short_title: IFG v Financial Ombudsman: fair compensation beyond legal causation limits
key_facts: IFG advised Mr and Mrs Jenkins to invest in high-risk FCS and Aspire currency funds despite their medium-risk requirement.
FCS losses were largely caused by unforeseeable fraud by the fund manager; IFG conceded Aspire was unsuitable but disputed liability for fraud losses.
Leading counsel's opinion based on South Australia Asset Management v York Montague held such losses were not recoverable at law.
Ombudsman Vaughan-Payne awarded full financial loss including fraud depletion as fair and reasonable though not legally mandated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Financial Ombudsman Service determination under the compulsory ombudsman scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the ombudsman lawfully took English causation law into account under Rule 3.8.1(2) and was entitled to award fair compensation departing from it.
enrichment.ratio: Section 228(2) FSMA requires determination by what is fair and reasonable, not strictly according to law; Rule 3.8.1(2) requires the ombudsman to take relevant law into account for both liability and quantum but permits a different result if that legal outcome would be unfair, provided the decision is not irrational.
legal_issues: Whether the ombudsman must apply English law on remoteness and causation in money awards
Whether Rule 3.8.1(2) applies to quantification as well as merits
Whether failure to articulate reasons for departing from law means law was ignored
Judicial review standard for fair-and-reasonable ombudsman determinations
linked_authorities: South Australia Asset Management Corp v York Montague Ltd [1997] AC 191
